title: HIV transition justice in Africa: A systematic scoping review of USAID/PEPFAR funding withdrawal, marginalized populations, and community-led HIV services
content:
by Ikekhwa Albert Ikhile, Ipeleng Pusetso Brodie

The 2025 reorganisation of United States foreign assistance exposed a structural vulnerability in African HIV responses: a donor may finance a modest share of national expenditure while supporting functions that determine whether marginalized populations can reach care. We conducted a systematic scoping review of peer-reviewed evidence on USAID/PEPFAR funding withdrawal, geographic reprioritisation, implementing-partner transition, and HIV-service disruption in Africa. Searches completed on 21 June 2026 were updated on 5 September 2026 through PubMed/MEDLINE via Europe PMC, Google Scholar, publisher platforms, and citation chaining. Of 543 records identified, 404 were screened, 94 full texts were assessed, and 30 studies were included: 24 empirical or programme-data studies, four modelling studies, and two reviews. We used design-sensitive credibility criteria informed by the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and separated observed outcomes from projections. Evidence from earlier transitions and the 2025 disruption converged on one finding: withdrawal is a layered health-system shock shaped by service domain, delivery architecture, political and legal context, fiscal capacity, and community participation. Treatment commodities may be protected while prevention, testing, outreach, peer navigation, psychosocial support, workforce, and monitoring contract—a prevention-treatment protection gap. Community-led organisations function as access, trust, intelligence, and accountability infrastructure; their loss can reduce services while erasing unmet need from routine data. We distinguish planned transition, abrupt suspension, and institutional dismantling because each requires different safeguards. The HIV Transition Justice Framework proposes six linked tests continuity, prevention, community, workforce, data, and sovereignty justice. African health sovereignty is the capability of African states, regional institutions, and communities to set priorities, finance and operate essential HIV functions, govern data, and hold decision-makers accountable without abandoning politically marginalized groups. Donor exit is not ethically neutral: it requires advance notice, co-designed transition, bridge financing, preservation of data and institutional memory, and safeguards against predictable inequitable harm.
